preamble: Nasalization of [u] to [ũ]. It usually comes from a following nasal consonant that is then lost, leaving its nasality on the vowel: Latin ūnum > Portuguese um [ũ], Proto-Balto-Slavic *-um > Old Lithuanian -ų [ũ]. It can also arise spontaneously, without an etymological nasal, as in Hindi ऊँट ū̃ṭ 'camel' from Prakrit uṭṭa. Lithuanian later denasalized ų to [uː]; Portuguese and Hindi keep the nasal vowel.

examples.note: The vowel took on nasality from the following n, which was then lost.
Final -um is pronounced as a nasal vowel with no consonantal nasal; the same outcome appears in atum [ɐˈtũ] 'tuna'.

examples.from: Sauraseni Prakrit uṭṭa, Old Hindi ऊट ūṭ 'camel' (< Sanskrit uṣṭra)
examples.note: Spontaneous nasalization with no etymological nasal; Wiktionary gives Old Hindi ऊट before the nasalized ऊंट.
Spontaneous nasalization; compare Punjabi ਉੱਚ ucc without nasality, while Bengali উঁচু ũcu shows the same nasal vowel.
The tautosyllabic n was lost before s and its nasality passed to the vowel, written ų. Modern Lithuanian later denasalized ų to [uː] ([ˈsʲuːsʲtʲɪ]).
Word-final *-um gave the nasal vowel ų, later denasalized to [uː].
